title: Cache Me If You Can
description: Cache Me If You Can is the 2013 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of djent about the ideas that run through every layer of a computer system. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword moves to an eight-string guitar, Wyrd lays down ambient synths, and Bytes plays polyrhythmic drums and growls the backing vocals. Caching, latency and bandwidth, bottlenecks, queues, state machines, leaky abstractions, virtual machines, containers, fault tolerance, availability, and the two hard things in computer science. The band toured as four virtual machines on one very loud server, until its fan failed and took everyone down at once. Play loud. Measure first.
tagline: The 2013 djent album from Procedural Byts: a systems fundamentals course in twelve songs, toured on four virtual machines and one very loud host.
lineup: The four-piece, virtualized. Nyble sings clean lead vocals on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays eight-string lead guitar. Wyrd plays ambient synths. Bytes plays polyrhythmic drums and sings harsh backing vocals.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, clean vocals and bass, and the one who changed the setlist. Three cached copies didn’t notice for a week.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits, now on an eight-string guitar. Eight strings, eight bits in a byte. Qword insists it’s a coincidence.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, on ambient synth pads, and the first member to move from a virtual machine into a container. It starts in one second. Wyrd mentions this often.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, polyrhythmic drums and growled backing vocals, and the one who played along with the stadium echo and slowed the whole show down.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Perfect uptime since 1970, mostly by not doing anything.

story.heading: One Very Loud Host
paragraphs: By 2013, the band’s tour rig weighed four tons. So they virtualized it: one enormous server on stage, running four virtual machines, one for each member’s gear. The label called it more reliable. Qword, meanwhile, moved to an eight-string guitar and insists that eight strings and eight bits in a byte is a coincidence.

On the first night, the server’s fan failed during the second song and all four virtual machines went down at once, in front of the whole crowd. Four machines, one point of failure. After that, there were two servers. That night became Fault Tolerant and Five Nines.

In stadiums, the sound from the far speakers arrived a quarter of a second late. Bytes started playing along with the echo instead of the beat, and the whole show slowed to a crawl until Nyble stamped the tempo back. That became Latency.
Halfway through the tour, Wyrd moved the synths out of a virtual machine and into a container. It started in one second. Everyone else’s took a minute. Wyrd has not stopped mentioning it.

The band cached the setlist on every member’s phone so nobody would need a signal backstage. Then Nyble changed a song, and three of the four cached copies kept the old one for a week. It was the four-setlist problem from 1992 all over again, and it became the closer, Two Hard Things.
Through all of it, one component of the rig never failed: Null. The duck has had perfect uptime since 1970, mostly by not doing anything.

cover_sub: The 2013 album. Toured as four virtual machines on one very loud host.

songs.title: Cache Me If You Can

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: The slow thing’s far away, so keep a copy near,
The answer that you just asked for, I’ve got it waiting here.
The processor, the browser, the name server down the street,
Every layer keeps a cache, so the trip is short and sweet!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Cache me if you can! (Hit!)
Cache me if you can! (Miss!)
Keep it close, keep it fast, keep the slow world at bay,
Cache me if you can, and I’m never far away!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The hit rate is the secret, how often it’s already there,
A miss goes all the way and costs you everywhere.
Least recently used goes out when the cache is full,
Memory, browser, network, it’s the same old pull!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: CPU cache! Page cache! Browser cache! DNS!
Content near the edge! Same idea, nothing less!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword keeps one short motif close at hand and fires it off instantly whenever it’s needed: a hit. When a phrase isn’t within reach, Qword has to go all the way down the neck to fetch it, and you can hear the wait: a miss.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Cache me if you can! (Hit!)
Cache me if you can! (Miss!)
Keep it close, keep it fast, keep the slow world at bay,
Cache me if you can, and I’m never far away!

songs.note: The band cached the setlist on every phone for this tour. That was the easy part.
songs.lesson: Caching keeps a copy of data close to where it’s used, so you don’t have to make the slow trip every time. It shows up at every layer of a system: CPU caches, the operating system’s page cache, browser caches, DNS caches and content delivery networks. How well it works depends on the hit rate, and when the cache is full, a policy like least recently used decides what to throw out.

songs.title: Latency

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Even light needs time to cross, it isn’t instant, no,
A round trip over the ocean’s a tenth of a second, slow.
The cache is nanoseconds and the memory’s a hundred more,
The disk is milliseconds, and the network’s out the door!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Latency! (How long to wait?)
Latency! (Even light is late!)
Not how much, but how long till the first byte arrives,
Latency, latency, the wait in all our lives!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Latency is how long it takes, and throughput is how much,
A pipe can be wide and still be slow to get in touch.
You can buy more bandwidth, but you can’t buy back the speed of light,
Move the data closer, and the waiting takes flight!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Nanoseconds! (Cache and memory!)
Milliseconds! (Disk and network!)
The speed of light! (The limit, can’t you see?)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays a simple pattern, and every hit comes back from the far speakers a quarter of a second late. He starts playing to the echo instead of the beat, and the whole band slows down with him, until Nyble stamps the tempo back.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Latency! (How long to wait?)
Latency! (Even light is late!)
Not how much, but how long till the first byte arrives,
Latency, latency, the wait in all our lives!

songs.note: In stadiums, the sound from the far speakers arrived a quarter of a second late. Bytes started playing to the delay, and the whole show slowed down.
songs.lesson: Latency is how long one operation or message takes, the time until the first byte arrives. Throughput is how much gets done per second. As a rough scale, a cache answers in nanoseconds, main memory in about a hundred, storage in micro- to milliseconds, and a network round trip across a continent in tens to hundreds of milliseconds, limited by the speed of light. You can buy more bandwidth, but latency mostly has to be designed around, by moving data closer.

songs.title: Bandwidth

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Send it down the wire and it’ll take a week or two,
Load a van with hard drives and drive it straight to you.
The van takes a day, but it carries so much more,
The bandwidth of a highway is the thing you’re looking for!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Bandwidth! (How much at once?)
Bandwidth! (Every second counts!)
A wide pipe moves the ocean, but the first drop takes its time,
Bandwidth, bandwidth, and latency’s a different line!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Throughput is the work that gets done in every hour,
Keep the pipe full of requests to use up all its power.
Overlap the waiting with more messages in flight,
Each one still takes as long, but the total’s out of sight!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: A van full of drives! (A week of wire!)
A day on the road! (And the bandwidth’s higher!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays the solo in huge eight-string chords, eight notes at a time, slow and wide. Each chord takes a while to arrive, but each one carries more than a fast single-note run ever could.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Bandwidth! (How much at once?)
Bandwidth! (Every second counts!)
A wide pipe moves the ocean, but the first drop takes its time,
Bandwidth, bandwidth, and latency’s a different line!

songs.note: Named after an old joke: never underestimate the bandwidth of a station wagon full of tapes hurtling down the highway. The band tested it with a van full of hard drives.
songs.lesson: Bandwidth, or throughput, is how much data moves per second, and it’s different from latency. A truck full of hard drives has enormous bandwidth but a very long latency; Andrew Tanenbaum made the joke about a station wagon full of tapes. You raise throughput by keeping many operations in flight at once, through pipelining or parallel requests, even though each one still takes just as long.

songs.title: Bottleneck

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I made the fast part faster and the show still ran as slow,
Because the slow part was the doorway everyone had to go.
The narrowest part decides how fast the whole thing flows,
Find the bottleneck first, and that’s where the time goes!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Bottleneck! (Find the slow part!)
Bottleneck! (Measure from the start!)
Don’t guess where the time is going, profile it and see,
Bottleneck, bottleneck, then fix the slowest for me!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Is it the CPU, the memory, the disk or the network line?
Measure it, don’t guess it, every single time.
Fix the worst, and then another bottleneck appears,
It moves around the system, and it’s been that way for years!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Profile! (Measure!) Benchmark! (Compare!)
Optimize the bottleneck! (Not the part that isn’t there!)

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble’s solo races along, but every phrase has to squeeze through one long, sustained note that can’t be hurried. Speeding up everything else changes nothing. Only when she shortens that one note does the whole solo get faster.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Bottleneck! (Find the slow part!)
Bottleneck! (Measure from the start!)
Don’t guess where the time is going, profile it and see,
Bottleneck, bottleneck, then fix the slowest for me!

songs.note: The band spent a week speeding up the wrong part of the show. Then they measured.
songs.lesson: A system is only as fast as its bottleneck, the most constrained resource, whether that’s the CPU, memory, disk, network or a single lock. Speeding up anything else barely helps. Measure with profilers and benchmarks instead of guessing, and expect a new bottleneck to appear as soon as you fix the old one.

songs.title: Queue Up

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A line at the counter and one person serving all,
At half full the line is short, the waiting time is small.
But fill it up to ninety and the line goes out the door,
The closer that you get to full, the wait grows more and more!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Queue up! (Wait your turn!)
Queue up! (Watch the waiting burn!)
Near a hundred percent busy and the line goes to the sky,
Queue up, queue up, and that’s the reason why!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: The number in the line is the arrival rate times the wait,
Little’s law, and it holds whether you’re early or you’re late.
Run a server at a hundred percent and the queue will never end,
Leave some room to spare, and the waiting starts to mend!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Fifty percent! (Short wait!) Ninety percent! (Too late!)
Ninety-nine percent! (Forever!) Leave some slack, and you’ll be great!

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes starts with plenty of space between hits. Every bar he adds more, filling the gaps, until at nearly full the pattern backs up and jams. He drops back to three-quarters, and it flows again.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Queue up! (Wait your turn!)
Queue up! (Watch the waiting burn!)
Near a hundred percent busy and the line goes to the sky,
Queue up, queue up, and that’s the reason why!

songs.note: The merch line at the first show moved fine until it was ninety percent full. Then it took two hours.
songs.lesson: Queueing theory explains why busy systems get slow so suddenly: as a server’s utilization approaches 100%, the waiting time doesn’t rise steadily, it shoots up. Systems need slack. Little’s law ties it together: the average number of things in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each one spends there. It applies to CPUs, disks, networks and checkout lines alike.

songs.title: State Machine

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A traffic light is red, then green, then yellow, then red again,
It only moves the ways it’s allowed, and it always knows when.
A state is where you are and an event is what comes in,
A transition takes you somewhere, and the cycle can begin!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: State machine! (Where am I now?)
State machine! (Where can I go, and how?)
States and transitions, and nothing in between,
State machine, state machine, the shape of every machine!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A vending machine is waiting, then it’s holding your coin,
Then it’s giving you a drink, then it’s waiting to rejoin.
A protocol, a parser, a door that’s locked or not,
Draw the states and arrows and you’ll see the whole plot!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Idle! (Coin!) Paid! (Button!)
Dispense! (Done!) And idle again, for everyone!

parts.label: Four states: full band
parts.desc: The solo has four sections, idle, building, peak and release, and the band can only move between them along the arrows drawn on the setlist. When Qword tries to jump straight from idle to peak, the band refuses.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: State machine! (Where am I now?)
State machine! (Where can I go, and how?)
States and transitions, and nothing in between,
State machine, state machine, the shape of every machine!

songs.note: Every section of this song is a state, and the band can only move between them in certain ways. They drew the diagram on the setlist.
songs.lesson: Many systems are best described as state machines: a fixed set of states, events that happen, and allowed transitions between states. Traffic lights, vending machines, network protocols like TCP, parsers and app screens all work this way. Drawing the states and arrows makes behavior explicit and exposes missing or impossible cases.

songs.title: Leaky Abstraction

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Every layer hides the one beneath, a promise and a wall,
You don’t need to know the details, you can trust it with it all.
But the file looks like it’s local till the network drops the line,
And the details leak right through the wall, and it’s no longer fine!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Leaky abstraction! (It hides, until it doesn’t!)
Leaky abstraction! (It was, until it wasn’t!)
Every layer’s a promise that it can’t completely keep,
Leaky abstraction, and the details seep!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Abstraction is the reason that we build such towering things,
Layers upon layers, each one with its promised strings.
So learn the layer underneath, at least a little bit,
Because one day it leaks, and you’ll have to deal with it!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: It’s just memory! (Until it pages!)
It’s just a call! (Until it crosses the network for ages!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays a smooth, clean melody, the abstraction, and every so often a harsh, distorted fragment breaks through underneath: the layer below, leaking through. By the end Qword has to play both at once.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Leaky abstraction! (It hides, until it doesn’t!)
Leaky abstraction! (It was, until it wasn’t!)
Every layer’s a promise that it can’t completely keep,
Leaky abstraction, and the details seep!

songs.note: The virtual machines were supposed to hide the hardware completely. Then the fan failed.
songs.lesson: Abstraction layers hide complexity behind simple interfaces, like files, sockets, virtual memory and SQL, and that’s how anyone builds large systems at all. But Joel Spolsky’s law of leaky abstractions (2002) says every non-trivial abstraction leaks: the hidden details, like latency, failures and performance, eventually show through. That’s why engineers need to understand at least a little of the layer underneath.

songs.title: Virtual Machine

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: One machine pretends to be four machines at once,
Each one thinks it owns the hardware, every single one.
The hypervisor sits beneath and slices up the core,
Gives each one its memory and walls between, and nothing more!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Virtual machine! (A computer in a computer!)
Virtual machine! (Isolated, no intruder!)
Run a different system in each one, side by side,
Virtual machine, virtual machine, and none of them collide!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Crash one and the others keep on running like before,
Copy it and move it, snapshot it, and restore.
Use the hardware better and fill the idle space,
But every layer costs a little, and you pay it in the race!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Hypervisor! (Underneath!) Guest! (On top!)
Isolation! (Walls!) And the host can never stop!

parts.label: Host and guests: full band
parts.desc: Bytes holds one massive groove: the host. On top of it, Nyble, Qword and Wyrd each play a completely separate part, as if the others weren’t there. Qword crashes out mid-phrase, and the other two keep going without missing a beat.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Virtual machine! (A computer in a computer!)
Virtual machine! (Isolated, no intruder!)
Run a different system in each one, side by side,
Virtual machine, virtual machine, and none of them collide!

songs.note: The band toured as four virtual machines on one very loud host.
songs.lesson: Virtualization runs several virtual machines on one physical computer. A hypervisor underneath divides up the CPU, memory and devices and keeps the machines isolated from each other, and each one runs its own operating system. Virtual machines use hardware more efficiently and can be snapshotted, copied and moved between hosts, at the cost of some overhead.

songs.title: Container

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A virtual machine boots a whole system of its own,
A container shares the kernel, lighter, faster, fully grown.
Pack the program with its libraries, everything it needs inside,
It runs the same on my machine, and on servers far and wide!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Container! (Pack it up!)
Container! (Ship it out!)
The same on my machine and yours, there isn’t any doubt,
Container, container, and it works throughout!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: It works on my machine, I said, and nobody believed,
Now my machine ships in the box, and everyone’s relieved.
Lighter isolation than a VM, a box inside the same,
Start a hundred in a minute, and they all play the game!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Virtual machine! (A minute!) Container! (A second!)
The same kernel! (Shared!) And the boot time’s reckoned!

parts.label: Synth solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd’s solo starts instantly, with no build-up, and then copies itself: one phrase, then four copies, then sixteen, all running at once, each sounding exactly like the first.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Container! (Pack it up!)
Container! (Ship it out!)
The same on my machine and yours, there isn’t any doubt,
Container, container, and it works throughout!

songs.note: Halfway through the tour, Wyrd moved the synths out of a virtual machine and into a container. It started in one second. Everyone else’s took a minute. Wyrd has not stopped mentioning it.
songs.lesson: Containers, made popular by Docker in 2013, package a program together with its libraries and settings and run it as an isolated process that shares the host’s operating system kernel. They’re much lighter and start much faster than virtual machines, which each run a whole operating system, but the isolation is weaker. They make software run the same way on every machine.

songs.title: Fault Tolerant

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Everything was on one machine, and the machine was very loud,
The fan stopped on the second song in front of the whole crowd.
Four virtual machines on a single host is one thing to fail,
One point of failure, and the whole show’s off the rail!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Fault tolerant! (Still standing!)
Fault tolerant! (Safe landing!)
Two of everything that matters, and when one goes, carry on,
Fault tolerant, fault tolerant, until the fault is gone!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Redundancy means a spare, a second one in place,
When the first one fails, the second takes its space.
Detect it, switch it over, and the audience won’t know,
No single point of failure, and on goes the show!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: It fails! (Detect it!) Failover! (Redirect it!)
Repair it! (Protect it!) Never one of anything! (Respect it!)

parts.label: Redundant pair: Qword and Nyble
parts.desc: Qword and Nyble play the exact same line in unison, each one the other’s backup. Halfway through, Qword stops dead, and Nyble carries the line alone without a gap. Nobody in the crowd notices.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Fault tolerant! (Still standing!)
Fault tolerant! (Safe landing!)
Two of everything that matters, and when one goes, carry on,
Fault tolerant, fault tolerant, until the fault is gone!

songs.note: On the first night of the tour, the host server’s fan failed and all four virtual machines went down at once. After that, there were two hosts.
songs.lesson: A fault-tolerant system keeps working when parts of it fail. The key is avoiding any single point of failure through redundancy: spare servers, disks, power supplies and network paths. Failures are detected and the system fails over to a backup automatically. The working assumption is that every component will eventually fail.

songs.title: Five Nines

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Ninety-nine percent sounds fine until you count the days,
Three and a half days down a year, and the crowd goes away.
Ninety-nine point nine is under nine hours lost,
Five nines is five minutes, and every nine has a cost!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Five nines! (Ninety-nine point nine nine nine!)
Five nines! (Five minutes down, that’s the line!)
Uptime over total time, and every nine’s ten times as hard,
Five nines, five nines, and always on guard!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Mean time between the failures and mean time to repair,
Make the failures rare and the fixes fast, and you’ll get there.
Every extra nine costs more, so choose the nines you need,
A hospital needs more than a blog, and that’s agreed!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Two nines! (Days!) Three nines! (Hours!)
Four nines! (An hour!) Five nines! (Five minutes of power!)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays a single pattern for the whole solo without a break, except for one tiny gap, a fraction of a beat, which he fills instantly. That gap is the five minutes a year. Everyone in the band heard it.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Five nines! (Ninety-nine point nine nine nine!)
Five nines! (Five minutes down, that’s the line!)
Uptime over total time, and every nine’s ten times as hard,
Five nines, five nines, and always on guard!

songs.note: Null has had perfect uptime since 1970, mostly by not doing anything.
songs.lesson: Availability is the fraction of time a system is working, usually counted in nines: 99% means about 3.65 days down per year, 99.9% about 8.8 hours, 99.99% about 53 minutes and 99.999% about 5 minutes. You improve it by making failures rarer (longer mean time between failures) and fixing them faster (shorter mean time to repair). Every extra nine costs far more than the last, so pick the level the service really needs.

songs.title: Two Hard Things

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: I changed a single song on the setlist on my phone,
But three of you had cached it, and the old one held its throne.
When the truth has changed, who tells the copies that they’re wrong?
That’s the hardest thing there is, and it’s been hard for long!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: There are two hard things! (Two hard things!)
Cache invalidation! (And naming things!)
And off-by-one errors! (That makes three!)
Two hard things, and the third one’s me!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Expire it after a while, or tell it when it’s changed,
Stale for a minute is fine, but stale all week is strange.
And naming things is hard, because a name’s a promise too,
And the off-by-one has followed us since nineteen seventy, through and through!

parts.label: Bridge (harsh vocals)
lines: Invalidate! (Tell the copies!)
Expire! (Let them go!)
Name it well! (Say what it is!)
Count from zero! (So you know!)

parts.label: Stale copies: full band
parts.desc: All four members play the same riff. Nyble changes one note, and the other three keep playing the old version, stale, until one by one they hear the change and update. The last one to catch up is one beat late: off by one.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: There are two hard things! (Two hard things!)
Cache invalidation! (And naming things!)
And off-by-one errors! (That makes three!)
Two hard things, and the third one’s me!

songs.note: The band cached the setlist on everyone’s phone. Nyble changed one song, and three of the four copies were wrong for a week. Third Normal Form all over again.
songs.lesson: A famous joke, usually credited to Phil Karlton, says there are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. People like to add a third: off-by-one errors. Cache invalidation is hard because cached copies go stale when the original changes; the usual fixes are expiring copies after a set time or telling caches explicitly when something has changed. Good names are what make a system understandable.
